mainTopic: Whose view the משנה follows on an individual who acted on a court's ruling, and how the majority of the קהל is defined and counted
overview: The גמרא first finishes proving that a ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, then brings רב נחמן in the name of שמואל, who says the משנה (an individual who follows the בית דין's mistaken ruling is פטור) is only רבי מאיר's view. It tries to prove this from a ברייתא where רבי מאיר exempts and the חכמים obligate. רב פפא and three איבעית אימא answers show the ברייתא can be read other ways, so the proof falls away. Next, רב אסי teaches from a פסוק that the majority of the קהל is counted only among those living in ארץ ישראל. The גמרא then asks what happens when the sinners change from a majority to a minority or the reverse, and shows that רבי שמעון requires both the sin and the finding out to happen at a time of obligation. A chain of questions asks whether two separate minorities can combine into a majority: the same חלב, two kinds of חלב, חלב and דם, and חלב and עבודה זרה. This chain ends in תיקו. Finally, the גמרא asks about a second court that repeats the ruling after the first court has died, and this question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns three exclusions from one verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting רבי יהודה, who reads three separate exclusions from the words 'זאת', 'העולה', and 'היא'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'This is the law of the burnt offering, it is.' These are three exclusions.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its proof that the ברייתא, which reads many exclusions from one verse, follows רבי יהודה, because רבי יהודה reads verses this way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the ברייתא learned several separate limits from the words of one פסוק. Here we see רבי יהודה doing the same thing with the פסוק about the עולה, finding three exclusions. Since the reading style matches, the ברייתא is likely his.

keyTerms.meaning: The law of the burnt offering
Exclusions: words in a פסוק that limit or leave something out

phrases.english: "This is the law of the burnt offering, it is"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 6:2

phrases.english: these are three exclusions.
phrases.notes: The three words are 'this', 'the burnt offering', and 'it is'; each one leaves out a different case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the earlier proof that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה's way of reading exclusions.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the ברייתא about the individual follows רבי יהודה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה's reading of three exclusions in ויקרא 6:2, matching the ברייתא's style.

steps.title: A second proof: the 'still I say' ברייתא cannot be רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: Another way to prove it: the ברייתא that begins 'עדיין אני אומר' says the בית דין brings the bull, which does not fit רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you want, say this: the ברייתא that says 'Still I say' cannot be explained as רבי יהודה's view, because it teaches: 'When most of the congregation sinned, the court brings a bull for them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different proof, built on a detail in the second ברייתא: who brings the bull.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the בית דין brings the פר on behalf of the sinning majority. If רבי יהודה holds that someone else brings it, then this ברייתא cannot be his. The next step shows what רבי יהודה actually holds.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: an introduction to an alternative explanation or proof
Still I say: the opening words of the ברייתא being discussed
You cannot set it up (explain it) as
A bull, here the communal sin offering

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
"Still I say"
phrases.notes: This names the ברייתא by its opening words, so we know which one is meant.

phrases.aramaic: לָא מָצֵית מוֹקְמַתְּ לַהּ כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: you cannot explain it according to Rabbi Yehuda,
since it teaches: a majority of the congregation that sinned,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין מְבִיאִין עַל יְדֵיהֶן פַּר,
phrases.english: the court brings a bull on their account,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, independent proof for the same conclusion as step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא 'עדיין אני אומר' is not רבי יהודה's.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's own wording that the בית דין brings the bull.

steps.title: רבי יהודה holds the tribes bring the bulls, not the court
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the ציבור brings the offering, not the בית דין, as the משנה says: seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if it were רבי יהודה, he said that the congregation brings the offering, not the court. As we learned in a משנה: רבי יהודה says, 'Seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the second proof by showing from a משנה that, for רבי יהודה, the tribes themselves bring the bulls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, each sinning tribe brings its own bull, so the people bring the offering, not the judges. The ברייתא said the בית דין brings the bull, so it clashes with רבי יהודה. That means it must follow a different תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: Seven tribes, meaning a majority of the twelve

steps.whatToRemember: For רבי יהודה, the communal sin offering is brought by the people (each tribe), not by the בית דין. So any source saying 'the court brings it' is not רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: But if it is Rabbi Yehuda, he said:

phrases.aramaic: צִבּוּר הוּא דְּמַיְיתֵי, בֵּית דִּין – לָא.
phrases.english: It is the congregation that brings it, not the court.
As we learned in a mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says:
Seven tribes that sinned
bring seven bulls.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source showing why the ברייתא in step 2 cannot follow רבי יהודה.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה holds the people, not the court, bring the bull.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה later in the מסכת: seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the משנה follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל says the משנה follows רבי מאיר, but the חכמים say an individual who acted on the court's ruling is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: This is the view of רבי מאיר, but the Rabbis say an individual who acted on the court's ruling is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new opinion about whose view the משנה represents: רבי מאיר, not רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the משנה (an individual who followed the בית דין is פטור) was matched to רבי יהודה. רב נחמן says instead that it is רבי מאיר's view, and the חכמים disagree. Either way, the חכמים hold the individual must bring his own offering.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable (here, to bring his own sin offering)

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions agree that the חכמים make the individual חייב. The only question is which תנא is behind the משנה that exempts him: רבי יהודה or רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
This is the view of Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: 'This' means our משנה, which exempts the individual.

phrases.english: but the Rabbis say:

phrases.aramaic: יָחִיד שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהוֹרָאַת בֵּית דִּין – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: an individual who acted on the ruling of the court is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different attribution for the משנה than the one argued for in steps 1-3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה exempting the individual is רבי מאיר; the חכמים hold such an individual is חייב.

steps.title: Where do רבי מאיר and the Rabbis argue?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we find this argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this 'רבי מאיר' and what is this 'Rabbis'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the argument that רב נחמן referred to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן mentioned an argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים but did not say where it appears. The גמרא wants to find the actual source.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis, the majority of sages

phrases.english: What is the view of Rabbi Meir, and what is the view of the Rabbis?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רב נחמן's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source where רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about this.

steps.title: The baraita: רבי מאיר exempts, the Rabbis obligate
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says: if they ruled and acted, רבי מאיר exempts and the חכמים obligate.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: If they ruled and acted, רבי מאיר exempts, and the Rabbis obligate.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא showing the argument between רבי מאיר and the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא records the argument, but it is short and does not say who did the act. That gap leads to the next question.

phrases.english: As it is taught: if they ruled and they acted,
Rabbi Meir exempts, and the Rabbis obligate.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא 'הורו ועשו': רבי מאיר פוטר, וחכמים מחייבין.

steps.title: Who did the act?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks who the 'they' are who acted in the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who acted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the ברייתא, setting up a check of each possibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'they ruled and they acted' could mean the judges themselves acted, or that someone else acted on their ruling. The גמרא will now test the options.

phrases.english: Who acted?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define the case in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity of those who performed the sin in the ברייתא.

steps.title: If the judges acted, why would the Rabbis obligate?
steps.stepSummary: If the בית דין themselves acted, the חכמים should not obligate, since a ברייתא says the action must be done by the קהל, while the ruling comes from the בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the court acted, what is the reason of the Rabbis who obligate? But it is taught in a ברייתא: You might think that if the court ruled and the court acted, they would be liable. The verse says 'the congregation... and they acted': the action depends on the congregation, and the ruling depends on the court.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first option, that the judges themselves acted, and challenges it from another ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא learns from the פסוק that a communal offering requires the קהל to do the act, while the בית דין gives the ruling. So if only the judges acted, no one should be חייב. That makes it hard to understand why the חכמים would obligate in that case, so the 'judges acted' reading looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say: introduces a possibility the גמרא is about to test
The action depends on the congregation

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a basic rule of the מסכת: for a communal offering, the בית דין gives the ruling and the people do the act. The judges alone cannot create the obligation.

phrases.english: If you say the court acted,
what is the reason of the Rabbis who obligate?
But isn't it taught: You might think that if the court ruled

phrases.aramaic: וְעָשׂוּ בֵּית דִּין, יָכוֹל יְהוּ חַיָּיבִין?
phrases.english: and the court acted, you might think they would be liable?
The verse teaches: "the congregation... and they acted,"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 4:13

phrases.english: the action depends on the congregation
and the ruling depends on the court!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא בֵּית דִּין, מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבָּנַן דִּמְחַיְּיבִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the first possible answer to step 7 and attacks it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'עשו' in the ברייתא means the בית דין themselves acted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא derives from 'הקהל ועשו' that the act must be done by the קהל, so judges acting alone would not be liable, which contradicts the חכמים obligating.

steps.title: Testing the case where a majority of the community acted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the ברייתא is about a majority of the community acting, but asks why רבי מאיר would then exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe the case is that the court ruled and most of the community acted on it? But then why would רבי מאיר say they are exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: Step 8 ruled out the option that the judges themselves acted. Now the גמרא tries a second option, a majority of the community acting, and immediately attacks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When most of the community acts on a mistaken ruling, the court is clearly obligated to bring an offering. So רבי מאיר's ruling of exempt makes no sense in that case. This option fails too, and that sets up the last remaining option.

phrases.english: Rather, perhaps the court issued a ruling
and the majority of the community acted on it.
If so, what is the reason of רבי מאיר
who exempts?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 8 rejected 'the בית דין acted,' this tests the next possible reading of 'they acted.'
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the ברייתא as a majority of the קהל acting
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In a majority case an offering is clearly due, so רבי מאיר could not exempt.

steps.title: The case must be a minority, so the argument is about an individual
steps.stepSummary: With the other options gone, the ברייתא must be about a minority acting. The argument is then whether an individual who follows the court is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it must be that the court ruled and only a minority of the community acted. They argue about exactly this: one opinion says an individual who acted on the court's ruling is exempt, and the other says he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles on the only reading left: a minority acted. This proves that רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about an individual acting on the court's ruling, which is what רב נחמן said in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A minority doesn't trigger the court's offering, so the question is whether each person brings his own. רבי מאיר says exempt, like the משנה. The חכמים say liable. This supports the claim that the משנה follows רבי מאיר alone.
steps.whatToRemember: At this point the גמרא has shown the dispute could be about an individual acting on the court's ruling, which supports רב נחמן in the name of שמואל.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not

phrases.aramaic: הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין וְעָשׂוּ מִיעוּט קָהָל,
phrases.english: that the court ruled and a minority of the community acted,
and this is what they disagree about:
One Sage holds:
phrases.notes: This is רבי מאיר.

phrases.aramaic: יָחִיד שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהוֹרָאַת בֵּית דִּין – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: An individual who acted on the court's ruling is exempt,
and the other Sage holds:

phrases.aramaic: יָחִיד שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהוֹרָאַת בֵּית דִּין – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: An individual who acted on the court's ruling is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The other two readings are gone, so this is the only one left, and it proves the point.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן's claim that the משנה follows רבי מאיר and the חכמים obligate an individual
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי מאיר and the חכמים, read as a minority case

steps.title: רב פפא: the argument is whether the judges count toward the majority
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says everyone agrees the individual is exempt. The argument is whether the judges join the community to make a majority.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Everyone agrees an individual who acted on the court's ruling is exempt. They argue whether the court counts together with the community to make up a majority. One opinion says the court completes the majority, and the other says it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא rejects the proof from step 10. He reads the same minority case a different way, so the ברייתא no longer shows that the חכמים argue on the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case, the community members who sinned are just short of a majority, but adding the judges who also sinned would make a majority. The חכמים count the judges, so an offering is owed. רבי מאיר does not count them, so no offering is owed. Both sides agree with the משנה about an individual.
steps.confusionAlert: רב פפא is not disagreeing with the משנה. He is saying the משנה is NOT only רבי מאיר's view, because even the חכמים agree that the individual is exempt.
steps.whyThisMatters: If רב פפא is right, the משנה's rule about an individual is accepted by everyone, not just רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Everyone agrees that

phrases.aramaic: יָחִיד שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהוֹרָאַת בֵּית דִּין – פָּטוּר,
phrases.english: an individual who acted on the court's ruling is exempt,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בֵּית דִּין מַשְׁלִים לְרוֹב צִבּוּר
phrases.english: but whether the court completes the majority of the community
is what they disagree about.

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר: בֵּית דִּין מַשְׁלִים לְרוֹב צִבּוּר,
phrases.english: One Sage holds: the court completes the majority of the community,
phrases.notes: This is the חכמים, so they say an offering is owed.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַר סָבַר: אֵין בֵּית דִּין מַשְׁלִים לְרוֹב צִבּוּר.
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: the court does not complete the majority of the community.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 10 by reading the minority case differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the חכמים argue on the משנה about an individual
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The minority case can be explained as an argument about counting the judges toward a majority, not about an individual's liability.

steps.title: Another answer: a real majority, and the חכמים are רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: the case is a real majority, and the 'חכמים' are רבי שמעון, who says both the community and the court bring offerings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: the court ruled and a majority of the community acted. Who are the חכמים? It is רבי שמעון, who said: the community brings an offering and the court brings an offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to push back on the proof. It goes back to the majority case from step 9 and explains it in a way that makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a majority case the court brings an offering. רבי מאיר exempts the community from bringing its own, while the 'חכמים', who are really רבי שמעון, say the community brings one too. So the argument is not about an individual, and the proof for רב נחמן falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you wish, say (an alternative answer)

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers push back on the proof. רב פפא says the argument is about counting the judges toward a majority. The איבעית אימא says it is a majority case and the חכמים are רבי שמעון. Either way, the ברייתא does not prove that the חכמים obligate an individual.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין וְעָשׂוּ רוּבּוֹ שֶׁל קָהָל,
phrases.english: the court ruled and a majority of the community acted,
and who are the 'חכמים'? It is רבי שמעון,
who said:
The community brings an offering and the court brings an offering.
phrases.notes: So the חכמים 'obligate' the community to bring its own offering in addition to the court's. רבי מאיר exempts the community.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate rejection of step 10's proof. It answers step 9's question about the majority case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the ברייתא's dispute is about an individual acting on the court's ruling
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The majority case does work if the חכמים are רבי שמעון, who requires an offering from the community as well as the court.

steps.title: A tribe following its own court, with רבי יהודה as the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: Another reading: the ברייתא is about one שבט that acted on its own court's ruling. The חכמים who obligate are רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say the case is a tribe that acted on its own court's ruling. Who are the 'חכמים'? It is רבי יהודה, as a ברייתא teaches: if a tribe acted on its own court's ruling, that tribe is obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to read the ברייתא. This weakens the earlier attempt to prove something from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this reading, the argument is about a single שבט following its own tribal court. רבי מאיר says that is not a real communal case, so there is no offering. The חכמים who obligate are רבי יהודה, who holds that such a tribe must bring an offering.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: an introduction to another answer
Its own court, meaning the tribe's local court

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
a tribe that acted on the ruling of its own court,
And who are the 'Rabbis'?
It is Rabbi Yehuda,
as it is taught in a baraita:
A tribe that acted on the ruling of its own court,
that tribe is obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: שֵׁבֶט שֶׁעָשָׂה בְּהוֹרָאַת בֵּית דִּינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another alternative reading of the ברייתא, parallel to Step 12
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא must be about a minority acting
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be about a tribe following its tribal court, with the חכמים being רבי יהודה

steps.title: Six tribes that are most of the people, or seven tribes that are not
steps.stepSummary: Another reading: the case is six tribes that are most of the population, or seven tribes that are not. The ברייתא's חכמים follow רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say the case is where six tribes sinned and they are most of the people, or seven tribes sinned even though they are not most of the people. Whose view is this teaching? It is רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more way to read the ברייתא. This time the argument is about how we count a 'majority'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A majority can be counted by tribes or by people. Six tribes can hold most of the people, and seven tribes are most of the tribes but may have fewer people. The obligating opinion counts either kind of majority, and that view belongs to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: Most of the community, counted by number of people
Six / seven tribes out of twelve

steps.confusionAlert: There are two kinds of 'majority' here. Six tribes are not most of the tribes, but they can be most of the people. Seven tribes are most of the tribes, even if they are fewer people.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
for example, where six tribes sinned,
and they are most of the people,
or seven tribes sinned,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינָן רוּבּוֹ שֶׁל קָהָל,
phrases.english: even though they are not most of the people,
and whose view is this teaching?
phrases.notes: Here 'מתניתין' means the ברייתא we have been discussing, not our משנה.

phrases.english: It is Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third alternative reading, parallel to Steps 12 and 13
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא must be about a minority acting
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument may be about how a majority is counted, by tribes or by people

steps.title: The ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the source: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, in רבי מאיר's name, obligates six tribes that are most of the people, or seven tribes that are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says in his name: if six tribes sinned and they are most of the people, or seven sinned even though they are not most of the people, they are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for the reading in Step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ברייתא shows that a real תנא counts either kind of majority, by people or by tribes. That makes the reading in Step 14 a real option. Since the ברייתא can be read so many ways, it gives no firm proof for the earlier claim.

keyTerms.meaning: In his name, meaning in רבי מאיר's name
They are obligated to bring an offering

steps.whatToRemember: Steps 11–15 each offer another way to read the ברייתא: רב פפא's reading and the three איבעית אימא readings. So it cannot prove the earlier claim that the משנה follows only רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in his name:
phrases.notes: 'His name' means רבי מאיר.

phrases.aramaic: חָטְאוּ שִׁשָּׁה וְהֵן רוּבּוֹ שֶׁל קָהָל,
phrases.english: if six tribes sinned and they are most of the people,
or seven tribes sinned

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינָן רוּבּוֹ שֶׁל קָהָל –
phrases.english: even though they are not most of the people,
they are obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the reading in Step 14
steps.raayaObject: That the obligating opinion can be רבי שמעון בן אלעזר
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר

steps.title: רב אסי: the majority is counted by those living in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רב אסי rules that for a mistaken court ruling, the majority is counted only by the residents of ארץ ישראל. He brings a פסוק about שלמה's חג.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אסי said: for a court ruling, follow the majority of those living in ארץ ישראל. As it says: 'And שלמה held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt, before ה׳ our God, seven days and seven days, fourteen days.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב אסי explains whose majority counts, and brings a פסוק that the גמרא will explain next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To be obligated, most of the קהל must act on the court's mistaken ruling. רב אסי says the counting includes only Jews living in ארץ ישראל, not those living outside it. The proof comes from how the פסוק describes the קהל.

keyTerms.meaning: A court ruling, here a mistaken one
Those who live in ארץ ישראל

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule decides who counts toward the majority that makes the community obligated to bring a פר העלם דבר של צבור.

phrases.english: Rav Asi said:
And for a court ruling, follow
the majority of those living in Eretz Yisrael,
as it is said:
'And Solomon held the feast at that time,'
phrases.notes: מלכים א 8:65

phrases.english: 'and all Israel with him, a great congregation,'
'from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt,'
phrases.notes: These are the northern and southern borders of ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: 'before ה׳ our God,'

phrases.aramaic: שִׁבְעַת יָמִים וְשִׁבְעַת יָמִים אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר יוֹם״.
phrases.english: 'seven days and seven days, fourteen days.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַסִּי: וּבְהוֹרָאָה, הַלֵּךְ אַחַר רוֹב יוֹשְׁבֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the ברייתא ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The majority for הוראה is counted by the residents of ארץ ישראל

steps.title: Why does the פסוק add 'from Hamath to the Brook of Egypt'?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק already said 'all Israel with him.' Why does it add 'a great congregation from Hamath to the Brook of Egypt'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, since it is written 'and all Israel with him,' why do I need 'a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that some words in the פסוק seem extra. It is setting up the lesson it will learn from them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'All Israel' already tells us everyone was there. So the added words that describe a קהל within the borders of ארץ ישראל must be teaching something new.

keyTerms.meaning: Now since: introduces a point the reader already accepts
Why do I need it? This asks about extra wording

phrases.english: Now, since it is written:
'and all Israel with him,'

phrases.aramaic: ״קָהָל גָּדוֹל מִלְּבוֹא חֲמָת עַד נַחַל מִצְרַיִם״
phrases.english: 'a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath until the Brook of Egypt'
why do I need it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רב אסי's פסוק proves his rule
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the extra words in the פסוק are teaching

steps.title: Only those living in ארץ ישראל are called 'קהל'
steps.stepSummary: From the extra words we learn that those in ארץ ישראל are called קהל, and those outside it are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this: these are the ones called 'קהל', but those are not called 'קהל'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the lesson from the extra words and proves רב אסי's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק attaches the word קהל to the people within the borders of ארץ ישראל. So the 'קהל' whose majority counts for הוראה means only those living in ארץ ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: draws a conclusion
These, the ones in ארץ ישראל / those, the ones outside it

steps.whatToRemember: For a mistaken court ruling, the majority of the קהל is counted only among Jews living in ארץ ישראל. This comes from 'קהל גדול מלבוא חמת עד נחל מצרים'.

phrases.english: Learn from this:
these are the ones called 'congregation,'
phrases.notes: 'These' means the people living in ארץ ישראל, between Hamath and the Brook of Egypt.

phrases.english: but those are not called 'congregation.'
phrases.notes: 'Those' means the Jews living outside ארץ ישראל.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: הָנֵי הוּא דְּאִיקְּרִי קָהָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 17 and proves רב אסי's rule
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only the residents of ארץ ישראל count as קהל for the majority needed in הוראה

steps.title: Many who became few: already covered by a known argument
steps.stepSummary: If a majority sinned and later became a minority, this is the argument between רבי שמעון and רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if the sinners were many and then became few, that is the argument between רבי שמעון and the Rabbis.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the simple case first: a majority sinned because of the ruling, then shrank to a minority. This sets up the harder question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known argument about a person whose status changes between the sin and the time he finds out. רבנן look at the time of the sin, so a sinning majority stays obligated. רבי שמעון looks at the finding out too, so once they are a minority there is no obligation.

keyTerms.meaning: They were many (a majority) and became few

phrases.english: It is obvious: if they were many and became few —
phrases.notes: "Many" means the sinners were a majority when they sinned, and later became a minority.

phrases.english: that is the argument of רבי שמעון and the Rabbis.
phrases.notes: This is their argument about a king or כהן גדול who sinned before being appointed and found out afterward.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining who counts toward the majority, the גמרא asks what happens if the majority changes over time.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A majority that sinned and then became a minority depends on the argument between רבי שמעון and רבנן.

steps.title: Few who became many: do they argue here too?
steps.stepSummary: If a minority sinned and later became a majority, does the same argument apply in the opposite direction?
steps.simpleTranslation: If they were few and became many, what is the law? Do רבי שמעון and the Rabbis argue here as well? רבי שמעון, who goes after the finding out, would obligate. The Rabbis, who go after the sin, would exempt. Or maybe not? What is it?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא asks about the reverse case: a minority sinned, and by the time they found out they had become a majority. It asks whether this fits neatly into the same argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we flip the argument, רבי שמעון would look at the finding out, when they are a majority, and obligate. רבנן would look at the sin, when they were a minority, and exempt. The question is whether that flip really works.

keyTerms.meaning: They were few (a minority) and became many
Finding out, becoming aware of the sin

phrases.english: If they were few and became many, what is the law?
Do רבי שמעון and the Rabbis argue here?

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּאָזֵיל בָּתַר יְדִיעָה מְחַיַּיב,
phrases.english: so that רבי שמעון, who goes after the finding out, obligates,
and the Rabbis, who go after the sin, exempt —
or not? What is it?
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוּעָטִין וְנִתְרַבּוּ, מַאי? מִי פְּלִיגִי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן וְרַבָּנַן?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the obvious case from step 19 and asks about its reverse.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the argument between רבי שמעון and רבנן also apply when a minority that sinned later becomes a majority?

steps.title: Does רבי שמעון really follow the finding out alone?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the question: רבי שמעון only looks at the finding out when the sin was also at a time of obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think so? Say you heard רבי שמעון goes also after the finding out, where both the finding out and the sin were at a time of obligation. But did you ever hear him say this when the finding out was at a time of obligation and the sin was not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the way the question in step 20 described רבי שמעון. It says we never heard him obligate someone based on the finding out alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the original case, the king or כהן גדול sinned as a regular person, which is also a time of obligation. So רבי שמעון only adds the finding out as an extra requirement. In the 'few became many' case, the sin happened while there was no obligation at all, since a minority does not bring the offering.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so? (pushing back on an assumption)

phrases.english: And can you really think so?
Say that you heard רבי שמעון
goes also after the finding out
[where both the finding out and the sin were at a time of obligation],
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording. They tell us when רבי שמעון looks at the finding out.

phrases.english: but finding out at such a time without the sin,
did you ever hear him say that?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיסְבְּרָא? אֵימוֹר דְּשָׁמְעַתְּ לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the description of רבי שמעון's view that the question in step 20 relied on.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי שמעון would obligate in the 'few became many' case because he follows the finding out.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי שמעון only counts the finding out when the sin also happened at a time of obligation. Here the sin happened with no obligation, so we cannot assume he obligates.

steps.title: Proof: otherwise they would bring the offering of their new status
steps.stepSummary: If רבי שמעון followed only the finding out, the king or כהן גדול should bring the offering of his new position, but he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if so, let him bring an offering according to his status now!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves its point from רבי שמעון's own ruling in the original case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only the finding out mattered, a king or כהן גדול who found out after being appointed would bring the offering of a king or כהן גדול. But רבי שמעון exempts him completely. That shows the finding out is not the only thing that counts.

keyTerms.meaning: According to now, his present status

phrases.english: For if so,
let him bring according to now!
phrases.notes: He means the king or כהן גדול should bring the offering that fits his new position.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the challenge in step 21 with a proof from רבי שמעון's ruling.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי שמעון does not decide based on the finding out alone.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי שמעון's ruling that a king or כהן גדול who found out after his appointment is exempt and does not bring the offering of his new status.

steps.title: רבי שמעון needs both the sin and the finding out
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון requires both the sin and the finding out to be at a time of obligation, so the 'few became many' case does not follow from the argument.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי שמעון requires both the sin and the finding out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא concludes that רבי שמעון needs both the sin and the finding out to happen at a time of obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So in the 'few became many' case, even רבי שמעון would not obligate, because the sin happened when they were a minority. The original question in step 20 is left without a clear answer.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, both the sin and the finding out must happen at a time of obligation. Following the finding out does not mean the finding out alone decides.

phrases.english: Rather, רבי שמעון
requires both the sin and the finding out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן חֲטָאָה וִידִיעָה בָּעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof in step 22.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי שמעון requires both the sin and the finding out to be at a time of obligation. So the 'few became many' case cannot simply depend on his argument with רבנן, and the question stays unresolved.

steps.title: Two minorities sin with forbidden fat after two separate rulings
steps.stepSummary: The בית דין twice rules that חלב is permitted, and each time a different minority eats it. Do the two minorities combine into a majority?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: The בית דין ruled that חלב is permitted, and a minority of the people ate it. Then the court took it back, ruled the same way again, and a different minority ate it. What is the law? Since there were two separate times of finding out, maybe they do not combine. Or perhaps, since both groups ate חלב, they do combine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. Two small groups each sinned because of a separate ruling, and it asks whether we count them together as one majority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whether the sinners are a majority or a minority matters, because only a majority of the קהל makes the communal offering for a mistaken ruling due. One side says the two rulings mean two separate times of finding out (ידיעות), so each group stands alone. The other side says it is the very same sin, eating חלב, so the groups can be added together.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the Sages)
Finding out (that one sinned); the plural means 'findings out'

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
The court ruled that forbidden fat is permitted,
and a minority of the congregation acted on it,
and the court took back their ruling,
and ruled again, and a different minority acted on it. What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דִּשְׁתֵּי יְדִיעוֹת נִינְהוּ לָא מִצְטָרֵף,
phrases.english: Since there are two separate findings out, they do not combine,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא: כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי חֵלֶב הוּא, מִצְטָרֵף?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since both this and that are forbidden fat, they combine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about whether two separate minorities can be added together into a majority.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do two minorities who sinned with the same חלב, after two separate rulings and two separate findings out, combine into a majority?

steps.title: Two minorities eat two different kinds of fat
steps.stepSummary: If the same חלב combines, what if one minority ate the fat on the stomach and the other ate the fat on the small intestines?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that since both are חלב they combine: what if one minority ate the fat on the stomach and the other minority ate the fat on the small intestines? Here, surely, since they come from two verses, they do not combine. Or perhaps, since both are חלב, they still combine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves one step further. Suppose we said 'yes' to the last question. It now asks about a case where the two groups ate two different kinds of חלב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last case was the same exact sin. Now the two fats are listed separately in the תורה, so maybe they count as two different sins. The other side says they are both still called חלב, so they combine.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (that the answer is...)

phrases.english: And if you say:

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי חֵלֶב הוּא מִצְטָרֵף,
phrases.english: since both this and that are forbidden fat, they combine,
then if a minority ate the fat that is on the stomach,

phrases.aramaic: וּמִיעוּט בְּחֵלֶב שֶׁעַל גַּבֵּי דַּקִּין, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: and a minority ate the fat that is on the small intestines, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי כֵּיוָן דְּבִתְרֵי קְרָאֵי קָאָתֵי – לָא מִצְטָרֵף,
phrases.english: Here, surely, since they come from two verses, they do not combine,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי חֵלֶב הוּא – מִצְטָרֵף?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since both this and that are forbidden fat, they combine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on a 'yes' answer to step 24 and makes the case harder: now the two fats are different.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do two minorities combine if each ate a different kind of חלב that comes from a separate verse?

steps.title: One minority eats fat and the other eats blood
steps.stepSummary: If the name חלב is enough to combine, what if one minority ate חלב and the other ate דם?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that the shared name חלב is enough and they combine: what if one minority ate חלב and the other ate blood? Here, surely, these are two different prohibitions, so they do not combine. Or perhaps, since their offering is the same, they do combine?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes one step further again. Now the two groups did two completely different sins, חלב and דם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now there is not even a shared name, because these are two separate prohibitions. The only thing in common is that the offering for each is the same. The question is whether a shared offering is enough to join the two groups.

keyTerms.meaning: Blood, which is forbidden to eat

phrases.english: And if you say:
it is all called forbidden fat, and so they combine,
then if a minority ate fat and a minority ate blood, what is the law?
Here, surely, they are two different prohibitions,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The words in square brackets in the next line are the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and since their prohibition is not the same, they do not combine,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן (דְּאִיסּוּרָן שָׁוֶה) – דְּקׇרְבָּנָן שָׁוֶה, מִצְטָרֵף?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since their offering is the same, they combine?
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the round-bracket words 'their prohibition is the same'. The point is only that the offering is the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on a 'yes' answer to step 25. Now the sins are two different prohibitions that share only the same offering.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is having the same offering enough to combine two minorities who broke two different prohibitions?

steps.title: One minority eats fat and the other serves idols
steps.stepSummary: If the same offering is enough, what if one minority ate חלב and the other did עבודה זרה, where neither the prohibition nor the offering is the same?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that since their offering is the same they combine: what if one minority ate חלב and the other did idol worship? Here, surely, neither the prohibition nor the offering is the same. Or perhaps, since both are punished with כרת, they do combine?
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last and furthest step in the chain. The two sins share no prohibition and no offering, only the punishment of כרת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עבודה זרה has a different offering than חלב, so even the link from the last step is gone. The only thing left in common is that both sins carry כרת when done on purpose. The question is whether that alone is enough to join the groups.

keyTerms.meaning: Being cut off, the heavenly punishment for certain sins done on purpose

phrases.english: And if you say:
since their offering is the same, they combine,
phrases.notes: Same as before: some versions leave out the round-bracket words.

phrases.aramaic: מִיעוּט בְּחֵלֶב וּמִיעוּט בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, מַהוּ?
phrases.english: then if a minority ate fat and a minority did idol worship, what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי אֵין אִיסּוּרָן שָׁוֶה וְאֵין קׇרְבָּנָן שָׁוֶה,
phrases.english: Here, surely, neither their prohibition nor their offering is the same, so they do not combine,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי כָּרֵת הוּא, מִצְטָרֵף?
phrases.english: or perhaps, since both this and that carry the punishment of כרת, they combine?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on a 'yes' answer to step 26. Now the only thing the two sins share is the punishment of כרת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a shared punishment of כרת enough to combine two minorities who did completely different sins?

steps.title: The questions stay unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the whole chain of questions with תיקו, meaning it is left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand unanswered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the chain of questions without deciding them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No answer was found, so none of the questions in steps 24 through 27 is decided. Because each question depended on a 'yes' to the one before it, the whole chain stays open, starting from the very first one.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question is left unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The ladder of questions goes: the same חלב, then two kinds of חלב, then חלב and דם (same offering), then חלב and עבודה זרה (only כרת in common). Each rung asks whether a weaker link can still join two minorities into a majority, and all of it ends in תיקו.
steps.confusionAlert: תיקו does not mean the answer is 'no.' It means the question was never decided.

phrases.english: Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the whole chain of questions from steps 24 to 27 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether separate minorities combine into a majority, at any level of connection, is left unresolved.

steps.title: A new court repeats the ruling and a second minority acts
steps.stepSummary: A בית דין rules חלב is permitted and a minority acts on it. That court dies, a new court gives the same ruling, and another minority acts. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: a court ruled that forbidden fat is permitted, and a minority of the people ate it. Then that court died, a new court took over, ruled the same thing again, and a different minority ate it. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It is like the earlier one, but now two different courts made the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier questions (steps 24-28), the same בית דין ruled both times. Here the first בית דין has died, and a new בית דין repeats the ruling. So the new issue is whether two minorities can join into one majority when the rulings came from two different courts.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the Sages)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with step 24. There, the same בית דין ruled twice. Here, a second court gives the ruling after the first one has died.

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
The court ruled that forbidden fat is permitted,
and a minority of the congregation acted on it,
and that court died
and another court arose in its place,
and they again issued the same ruling,
and a different minority acted on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: הוֹרוּ בֵּית דִּין שֶׁחֵלֶב מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the תיקו in step 28, the גמרא opens a new question. It changes step 24's case from one court to two different courts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether two minorities who acted on the rulings of two different courts combine into a majority.

steps.title: No question if the court brings the offering
steps.stepSummary: If the בית דין is the one who brings the offering, there is nothing to ask. The first court is no longer alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says the court brings the offering, you can't ask this question, because they (the first court) are not here anymore.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the question. It shows that under one opinion, the question doesn't even start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the offering belongs to the בית דין, then the first court would have to bring it. That court has died, so it cannot bring anything. The two minorities can't be joined under one court's offering, so there is nothing to ask.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
You should not ask this question
They are not here (no longer exist)

phrases.english: According to the one who says
the court brings the offering –
do not ask the question,
since they are no longer here,

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר בֵּית דִּין מַיְיתֵי לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the question from step 29. It shows the question doesn't apply under the view that the בית דין brings the offering.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under the view that the בית דין brings the offering, there is no question, because the first court no longer exists.

steps.title: The question only matters if the congregation brings the offering
steps.stepSummary: The question really applies according to the view that the צבור brings the offering. The first side is that the people still exist, so maybe the two minorities combine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when should you ask? According to the one who says the congregation brings the offering. What is the law? The congregation is still here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves the question to the opinion where it actually makes sense. Then it starts laying out the first side of the doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the צבור brings the offering, the courts dying doesn't matter, because the people are still alive. Taken together, the two minorities make up a majority of the people who sinned. That is the first side of the question. The other side continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, when should you ask the question?

phrases.english: Rather, when should you ask the question? –
according to the one who says the congregation brings the offering,
what is the law? The congregation still exists,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר צִבּוּר מַיְיתֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 30 ruled out one opinion, this step moves the question to the opinion where it applies. It begins presenting the first side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Under the view that the צבור brings the offering, do the two minorities combine into a majority even though two different courts ruled, since the people still exist?
